opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the key thing to understand is that TensorLogic isn't really an architecture in the narrow sense, like a transformer or a convnet. It's more of a language, a single construct that I think underlies both deep learning and symbolic AI. That construct is the tensor equation.

The observation that started all of this is that a logical rule, say a Datalog rule where you join two relations and project out some variables, is mathematically the same operation as an Einstein summation over tensors. A relation is just a sparse Boolean tensor. Joining relations is multiplying tensors along shared indices. Projecting out a variable is summing over that index. So the thing that symbolic AI people have been doing for fifty years and the thing deep learning people do every day on GPUs are really the same thing in different clothing.

Once you see that, gradient descent becomes very natural. Everything in TensorLogic is a tensor equation, and tensor equations are differentiable. You don't have to bolt on some special trick to make your logic learnable, or some special trick to make your neural network interpretable. You write the program, and the gradient of the program is itself a program in the same language. That's a very powerful closure property. In most systems you have one world for the model and another world for learning. Here they're the same.

The other big piece is what happens when you go from Boolean tensors to real-valued ones. If you take a logical rule and let its tensors become embeddings, with a temperature parameter, you get a continuous spectrum. At zero temperature you have pure deductive reasoning, with no hallucinations, because you're just doing logic. As you raise the temperature you get analogy and generalization, the kind of soft similarity-based reasoning that neural nets are good at. Gradient descent can then learn the embeddings and the structure, and you still have a system that you can read and reason about.

So why do I think it's powerful? Because it gives gradient descent something it has always lacked: a representation where what's learned is transparent and composable, where you can mix in knowledge you already have, and where reasoning is reliable when you need it to be. Current deep learning is basically learning without much reasoning, and classic AI was reasoning without much learning. TensorLogic is my attempt to say you don't have to choose. It's one language, one operation, and gradient descent works on all of it.

r002.rationale: It describes moving from Boolean tensors to real-valued tensors as temperature changes, but does not state that thresholding a learned numeric representation into Boolean form reveals the learned concept.

r003.rationale: The response praises TensorLogic’s representation and says gradient descent works on it, but does not identify the architecture gradient descent operates on as a condition for its ability to learn powerful representations.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the key insight behind Tensor Logic is that the two things people think of as fundamentally different, logical reasoning and neural computation, are actually the same operation. A rule in logic, something like "X is the grandparent of Z if X is the parent of Y and Y is the parent of Z," is really a join followed by a projection. And in tensor terms, a join is a product and a projection is a sum. So a logical rule is just an Einstein summation, a tensor contraction. Once you see that, the whole dichotomy between symbolic AI and neural networks dissolves.

Now, why does that matter for gradient descent? Because in the standard neural world, you can only learn things that you've expressed as differentiable operations, and the structure you can impose is pretty impoverished. You've got matrix multiplies, you've got nonlinearities, and you hope the model figures out the rest. In Tensor Logic, every piece of knowledge you have, every rule, every constraint, every piece of structure, becomes a tensor equation that is differentiable by construction. So you can write down what you know, and then gradient descent fills in what you don't. The weights in those tensors are learnable parameters just like any other.

And there's a deeper point. In classical logic, inference is brittle. A single wrong fact, and everything downstream collapses. In a neural network, you have the opposite problem: it's robust but it hallucinates, it can't reason reliably. With Tensor Logic you get a dial. At one extreme, with hard thresholds, you have sound, deductive reasoning with no hallucination, because the system literally cannot derive anything that doesn't follow. Move the temperature up and you get something that generalizes, that does analogy, that behaves like an embedding-based model. And the whole thing is one language, one set of equations, so gradient descent can flow through all of it, from the raw perception at the bottom to the abstract reasoning at the top.

I'd also say it's powerful in a very practical sense. Transformers, graphical models, kernel machines, logic programs, you can write each of them in a few lines of Tensor Logic. It's a small language, there's really only one construct in it, but it's expressive enough to cover everything we do in AI today. And when you have one language that unifies learning and reasoning, you stop having to bolt things together. You're not calling a symbolic solver from a neural net or vice versa. You're just optimizing one object, and gradient descent is the engine that drives it.

r002.rationale: It describes hard thresholds as enabling sound deductive reasoning, but does not say thresholding a learned numeric representation reveals the concept it learned.

r003.rationale: It contrasts the limited structures of standard neural architectures with TensorLogic’s richer differentiable structure, tying what gradient descent can learn to the architecture it operates on.

astra-6.text:
The key idea is that tensors and logic give you two complementary ways to describe a computation. Tensors give you the numerical machinery that makes neural networks work, while logic gives you a way to express relationships, rules, and how computations fit together. TensorLogic brings those into the same framework.

Why is that useful for gradient descent? Because, when you express those relationships through differentiable tensor operations, you can learn the parameters of the resulting computation end to end. You can put structure into the model instead of asking gradient descent to discover everything from scratch.

But there’s an important distinction: gradient descent doesn’t magically optimize arbitrary discrete logical choices. You need a differentiable parameterization or an appropriate relaxation. The power is in being able to combine explicit structure with learning, so that what you know guides what you learn.

sol-6.1.text:
Because it gives you a common language for neural networks and logical reasoning. In TensorLogic, you express computations as operations on tensors, but those operations can also have a logical interpretation. So you can bring rules and relationships into the same framework as learned representations.

The important point about gradient descent is that it’s an optimization method, not a commitment to a particular neural network architecture. If you build a differentiable computation, you can propagate gradients through it. That opens up a much larger space of models than the architectures we typically train today.

And knowledge can help shape that space. Instead of asking gradient descent to discover everything from examples, you can supply some of the structure and learn what you don’t know. You still have to make appropriate choices about differentiability and optimization—it doesn’t magically solve those problems—but you have a framework in which learning and reasoning can work together.
